source: Bainbridge (1983) Ironies of Automation
finding: Automating a process does not remove the human. It leaves the operator the tasks the designer could not automate, and makes those tasks harder. The more advanced the control system, the more crucial the human contribution.
numbers: Qualitative argument, no sample. Cites vigilance work (Mackworth 1950): effective attention to a low-event source fails after about half an hour.
quote: The operator can be left with an arbitrary collection of tasks, and little thought may have been given to providing support for them.
limits: Position paper from process control and flight decks. Little data of its own. Authors of error data were 'reluctant to publish'.
agent_relevance: Our program/model split is an automation. The model is left the unautomatable parts (open slots), so those parts need the most care, not the least.

source: Bainbridge (1983) Ironies of Automation - monitoring irony
finding: A human asked to monitor a computer that does the job better cannot check it in real time. At best they judge its decisions at a meta-level. Monitoring a rarely-failing system also decays.
numbers: Rule: if decisions can be fully specified the computer is faster and more accurate, so the monitor 'has been given an impossible task'. Cites Ephrath (1980): aided performance was worse than unaided because the operator decided anyway and checking added workload.
limits: Argument from cases, not a controlled test. Ephrath result is cited second-hand.
agent_relevance: A model checking a program's output, or a human checking a model's long output, hits the same limit. Checks must be code-run, not judged (matches G2, G5).

source: Bainbridge (1983) Ironies of Automation - skill loss and take-over
finding: Manual skill and the 'running memory' of process state decay when the operator only watches. Take-over happens when the process is abnormal, so the operator then needs more skill, not less.
numbers: Operators come in 15 to 30 minutes before taking over to build a picture of the process. Very fast failures (seconds) need reliable automatic response.
limits: 1983 process-control setting. Time figures are anecdotal.
agent_relevance: When the scaffold hands control back to the model after a failed check, the model has no running state. Pass the failing output and a state summary explicitly (G2).

source: Bainbridge (1983) Ironies of Automation - collaboration and the Fitts list
finding: The static Fitts-list view (give each side what it is best at) is called insufficient. It ignores integration and keeping the operator's skill alive. Proposes computer support that keeps the human on-line, and says the computer's decision methods should be ones the operator can follow.
numbers: Lists four advice types (Thompson 1981): causes, importance, alternatives, how to implement. Says following advice makes reactions slower and less integrated than generating the sequence oneself.
limits: Design advice, not tested in the paper. Some claims cite earlier lab work.
agent_relevance: Supports a design where each program step is inspectable by trace. Warns that a fixed role split ('program decides, model fills') still needs a feedback path.

source: Wikipedia: Cognitive systems engineering (history and references)
finding: CSE came out of Three Mile Island (1979). Hollnagel and Woods named it in 1983 ('New wine in new bottles', Int J Man-Machine Studies). They moved the unit of analysis from the person to the joint cognitive system: people plus technology treated as one entity that does cognitive work.
numbers: Reference list gives: Hollnagel and Woods 1983; Bainbridge 1983; Woods 1984 (visual momentum); Woods 1995 (alarm problem); Hutchins 1995; Rasmussen, Pejtersen and Goodstein 1994; Hollnagel and Woods 2005 (Foundations); Woods and Hollnagel 2006 (Patterns); Klein et al 2004, 2005; Hollnagel 2012.
limits: Secondary encyclopedia page, which itself notes the book years vary (2005, 2006, 2019). I did not open the 1983 paper or the books.
agent_relevance: Gives the citation trail. The key idea for us is the unit of analysis: score the pair (program + model), not the model.

source: Hollnagel and Woods (1983) Cognitive systems engineering: new wine in new bottles
finding: Introduced CSE and the joint cognitive system. A cognitive system is defined by what it does (keeps control of its performance using knowledge and anticipation), not by what it is made of. Human and machine are one system if together they keep control.
numbers: Not opened. No figures.
limits: Paywalled, not opened. Description rests on the secondary page and common citation; check against the full text before relying on wording.
agent_relevance: A functional definition fits an agent: scaffold plus model counts as one controller if the pair keeps control of the task.

source: Hollnagel and Woods (2005) Joint Cognitive Systems: Foundations of CSE; Woods and Hollnagel (2006) Patterns in CSE (books)
finding: Core claims recalled from the book pair: study the pair as one system; use the contextual control model (COCOM) with control modes scrambled, opportunistic, tactical and strategic, set by available time and competence; describe by function, not structure.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers; the books are qualitative.
limits: Books not opened. COCOM mode names are from memory and unverified here. Treat as [S] until checked.
agent_relevance: Control modes could map to budget-driven behaviour: little time means narrow opportunistic moves; more time allows planning.

source: Wikipedia: Automation bias (empirical figures)
finding: Automation bias shows as omission errors (missing what the aid misses) and commission errors (following a wrong aid). Teams do not remove it. Training reduced commission but not omission errors. Accountability reduced bias. Varying reliability reduced complacency.
numbers: Cited figures: breast cancer detected in 46% of cases without aids vs 21% of cases when the aid missed the cancer; clinician accuracy rose 29% to 50% with decision support but 7% of answers right without it were changed to wrong. No sample sizes given.
limits: Encyclopedia summary; primary studies (Mosier, Skitka, Parasuraman) not opened.
agent_relevance: The 'aid misses, human misses too' pattern equals correlated errors between a model and its checker. Do not let a model verify a model's answer alone (G4).

source: Vaccaro, Almaatouq and Malone (2024) When are combinations of humans and AI useful? Meta-analysis
finding: Across 106 experiments and 370 effect sizes (2020 to mid-2023), human-AI teams did worse than the better of human alone or AI alone. They did beat humans alone.
numbers: Synergy vs best single: Hedges g = -0.23 (95% CI -0.39 to -0.07, p=0.005). Augmentation vs human alone: g = 0.64 (CI 0.53 to 0.74). Heterogeneity I2 = 97.7% (synergy). 74 papers kept from 5126 screened.
limits: Mostly short lab tasks with crowd workers; window ends mid-2023 so it excludes newer LLM assistants. Pre-registered.
agent_relevance: Pairing is not automatically better. A scaffold that adds steps must be tested against the model alone (our plain arm), as the harness already does.

source: Vaccaro et al. (2024) moderators: task type and who is better alone
finding: Decision tasks lost, creation tasks gained. When the human was better alone the team gained; when the AI was better alone the team lost.
numbers: Decision tasks g = -0.27 (CI -0.44 to -0.10); creation tasks g = 0.19 (CI -0.09 to 0.48, n.s., n=34); difference p=0.006. Human better alone: g = +0.46 (CI 0.28 to 0.66). AI better alone: g = -0.54 (CI -0.71 to -0.37). Explanations, confidence display, participant type and division of labour were not significant moderators.
limits: Creation-task gain is not itself significant. Moderators are correlational across studies, not manipulated.
agent_relevance: Where the model beats the checking human, adding human judgment hurts. Supports 'code selects' and a narrow role for judged steps.

source: Bansal et al. (2021) Does the whole exceed its parts? AI explanations and complementary team performance (CHI)
finding: With an AI whose accuracy is comparable to humans, teams in all conditions beat the human alone and showed complementary performance. Explanations did not add accuracy over just showing confidence. Explanations raised the chance people accept the AI, right or wrong.
numbers: Three tasks (Beer and Amzbook sentiment, LSAT), about 100 participants per condition. Explanation vs confidence: no significant gain (for example LSAT adaptive-expert vs confidence stat 0.16, p=.87). Explain-Top-1 worsened accuracy when the AI was wrong. Prior studies in its Table 1: deceptive reviews human 51.1%, AI 87.0%, team 74.6% (team below AI alone).
limits: MTurk workers; AI accuracy deliberately matched to humans to leave room for complementarity. Not a field setting. Adaptive explanation gave suggestive, not significant, gains.
agent_relevance: A persuasive rationale from the model makes a reader more likely to accept it. Do not show model rationale to a judge or checker without a code-run check (G5).

source: Bucinca, Malaya and Gajos (2021) To trust or to think: cognitive forcing functions (CSCW)
finding: Forcing people to think before seeing the AI answer (or delaying it) cut overreliance but did not remove it. The designs that worked best were the ones people liked least and trusted least.
numbers: 199 participants analysed, simulated AI with 75% accuracy, nutrition task. When the AI was wrong, mean correct rate: no-AI 0.18, simple explainable AI 0.03, forcing functions 0.09 (carb source detection: 0.49, 0.08, 0.27). Effect size forcing vs simple d = 0.37 (overall), 0.66 (carb source). High need-for-cognition people gained more.
limits: MTurk; simulated AI; one task domain; 260 recruited, 49 excluded by a 55% invalid-answer rule and 12 more removed.
agent_relevance: Closest human-side analogue to a gate: make the reader commit before seeing a proposed answer. Our G5 (judge sees no proposed answer) is the same move for a model judge.

source: Vasconcelos et al. (2023) Explanations can reduce overreliance on AI systems (CSCW)
finding: Overreliance is a strategic cost-benefit choice, not a fixed bias. Explanations reduce it only when they make checking cheaper than just trusting the AI. This may explain null explanation effects in earlier work such as Bansal 2021.
numbers: Five studies, total N = 731 (Study 1 N=340 task difficulty; Study 2 N=340 and Study 3 N=286 explanation difficulty; Study 4 N=114 money; Study 5 N=76 effort discounting). Maze task, simulated AI at 80% accuracy. Easy task: explanation did not change overreliance; hard task: it fell with explanation. Harder-to-read written explanations raised overreliance.
limits: Prolific, maze task, simulated AI. Generalisation to open tasks untested. Subject totals overlap across studies as reported.
agent_relevance: Verification effort is the lever. For a model agent too, make the check cheap and mechanical (run it) so it is actually used.

source: Hemmer et al. (2024) Complementarity in human-AI collaboration: concept, sources, evidence
finding: Formal model of complementarity. Potential splits into inherent (one side is right where the other is wrong) and collaborative parts. Two sources: information asymmetry and capability asymmetry. Realising the potential depends on knowing which side to trust per case.
numbers: Study with a complementary AI: inherent potential 0.2480 vs baseline AI 0.0640 (d=3.81, p<0.001). Share of potential that was inherent: 24% baseline, 93% complementary. Share of inherent potential realised: 58% baseline, 89% complementary AI (d=3.43, p<0.001).
limits: Two lab studies; sample sizes not extracted here. Binary decision tasks.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable target for the program/model split: count cases where only one side is right, and how often the selector picks the right one.

source: Simkute et al. (2024) Ironies of generative AI: understanding and mitigating productivity loss
finding: Applies Bainbridge's ironies to LLM tools. Four causes of productivity loss: shift from producing to evaluating, restructured workflows, interruptions, and automation making easy tasks easier and hard tasks harder. Proposes continuous feedback, ecological interface design, task stabilisation and clear task allocation.
numbers: No new data. Synthesises user studies, for example Vaithilingam et al.: Copilot users failed tasks more often and were no faster than with plain autocomplete.
limits: Narrative review, no meta-analysis, study selection not systematic.
agent_relevance: The four causes are a checklist for our scaffold: does each step turn the model's job into evaluation, break its sequence, or interrupt it?

source: Mozannar et al. (2022, rev. 2024) Reading between the lines: modeling user behavior and costs in AI-assisted programming (CUPS)
finding: A taxonomy of programmer states with Copilot (CUPS), labelled by 21 programmers on their own sessions. Much time goes to thinking about and verifying suggestions, including verification after acceptance.
numbers: 21 participants. 'I don't know' segments were 6.5% of session time. When a programmer accepts a suggestion without full checking, they verify it right afterward 53.2% of the time; mean verification time including that post-hoc part is 15.21 s (median 6.48 s), nearly five times the naive figure.
limits: Small sample, self-labelled after the fact, one tool, 2022 model.
agent_relevance: Verification is the hidden cost of the pair. Log verification time per step in our harness, not only model calls.

source: Peng et al. (2023) The impact of AI on developer productivity: evidence from GitHub Copilot
finding: Randomised trial: write an HTTP server in JavaScript. The Copilot group finished faster.
numbers: 95 developers (of 166 invited). Mean time 71.17 min with Copilot vs 160.89 min control: 55.8% faster, 95% CI 21% to 89%, p=0.0017. Both groups predicted only about 35% gain.
limits: One short, well-specified task; wide CI; four outliers noted; speed only, no quality measure.
agent_relevance: The best-case end of the range (greenfield, short task). Compare with METR, same tool class, opposite sign.

source: METR (2025) Measuring the impact of early-2025 AI on experienced open-source developers
finding: Randomised trial on real issues in mature projects. Allowing AI made experienced developers slower, though they believed it sped them up.
numbers: 16 developers, 246 tasks (about 2.0 h each). Forecast before: AI saves 24% time. Estimate after: saved 20%. Measured: 19% more time with AI. Experts predicted 39% (economists) and 38% (ML) shorter.
limits: Only 16 developers, highly skilled in their own repos; tools were Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet; authors say experimental artifacts cannot be fully excluded; 21 candidate causes examined.
agent_relevance: Felt speed-up and measured speed can differ in sign. Judge the pair by measured outcome, never by self-report (G2 spirit).

source: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond (2023) Generative AI at work (NBER 31161)
finding: Staggered rollout of an AI conversational assistant to customer support agents. Productivity rose on average, mostly for novices, little for experts.
numbers: 5,179 agents. Issues resolved per hour +14% on average; +34% for novice and low-skilled workers; minimal impact on experienced, highly skilled workers.
limits: One firm, one tool, one task type; working paper, not peer reviewed in this version; throughput measure.
agent_relevance: Matches the Vaccaro moderator: the weaker partner gains most. A weak model with a strong scaffold may gain more than a strong model.

source: Lee et al. (2025) The impact of generative AI on critical thinking: survey of knowledge workers (CHI)
finding: Self-reported: higher confidence in GenAI goes with less critical thinking; higher self-confidence goes with more. GenAI shifts effort from gathering and producing toward verifying and integrating.
numbers: 319 knowledge workers sharing 936 first-hand examples of GenAI use at work; 96.87% of the sample used ChatGPT among their top tools; all used GenAI at work at least weekly.
limits: Self-report survey, not behaviour; correlational.
agent_relevance: The human half of the pair drifts toward trust when the tool looks good. Design gates that do not rely on the human choosing to look.

source: Shaikh et al. (2024) Grounding gaps in language model generations (NAACL)
finding: LLMs presume common ground instead of building it. They produce far fewer clarification, follow-up and acknowledgment acts than humans. Preference optimisation makes this worse.
numbers: With GPT-3.5 across dialogue sets: follow-ups down 64.3% on average, acknowledgments down 83.4%, clarification down 84.8% on one set and never produced on two others. Mistral 7B: PPO cut the base rate by 7.0% and agreement by 39.0%; DPO cut the base rate by 12.1% and agreement by 42.5%. Grounding acts were present in 11.83% of UltraChat and 18.35% of UltraFeedback samples.
limits: Simulated turn-taking against human dialogue datasets, mostly 2023 models; one exception (GPT-3.5 instruct) matched the human rate (29.5 vs 27.9).
agent_relevance: Klein's 'common ground' need for a good team player is not met by default. The scaffold should ask for missing information in code, not hope the model asks.

source: Shao et al. (2026) Collaborative Gym: framework for human-agent collaboration (ICLR 2026; arXiv Dec 2024)
finding: Collaborative LM agents beat fully autonomous ones when judged by real users, but fail often at communication and situational awareness. In simulation, teams delivered less often but at higher quality.
numbers: Win rates over autonomous agents: 86% Travel Planning, 74% Tabular Analysis, 66% Related Work. Failures: communication in 65% and situational awareness in 40% of real-condition cases (simulated: 80% and 47%). Users spend 21 to 32% of actions on direct environment control.
limits: Three tasks, four LMs, user simulator plus a real condition of modest size; win rates come from user preference ratings.
agent_relevance: A direct LLM test of the joint-system idea: the pair wins, and the weak link is coordination, not task skill. Needs explicit status and progress messages from the program.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan and Griffiths (2024) Cognitive architectures for language agents (CoALA, TMLR)
finding: Framework that splits a language agent into memory modules (working, episodic, semantic, procedural), an action space (internal and external) and a decision procedure that selects among actions. The LLM is one component inside a program-controlled cycle.
numbers: Conceptual framework; no benchmark numbers.
limits: Descriptive taxonomy of existing agents; makes no performance claim.
agent_relevance: Closest formal statement of our split: a program owns the decision loop and the memory, the model is a callable. Use its vocabulary when naming schema states.

source: Shneiderman (2020) Human-centered AI: reliable, safe and trustworthy
finding: Replaces the one-dimensional Sheridan-Verplank levels of automation (1978) with two independent axes: level of computer automation and level of human control. The goal is both high.
numbers: Two-axis framework, no experiments. Notes Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens (2000) refined the levels by stage.
limits: Normative framework; evidence is by example.
agent_relevance: Separate how much the program automates from how much the user can inspect and override. Our design can be high on both: program decides, every step shown and overridable.

source: Dell'Acqua et al. (2023) Navigating the jagged technological frontier (HBS working paper 24-013)
finding: Field experiment with consultants and GPT-4. On tasks inside the AI's frontier, quality and speed rose. On a task outside the frontier, those using AI were less often correct.
numbers: Recalled, not opened: 758 BCG consultants; inside frontier about 12% more tasks, 25% faster, over 40% higher quality; outside frontier about 19 percentage points less likely to be correct.
limits: NOT OPENED (download failed). Numbers are from memory and must be verified before use.
agent_relevance: The jagged frontier: the pair can be worse than the human alone exactly where the model is confidently wrong. Fits Vaccaro's AI-better/human-better split.

source: Klein, Woods, Bradshaw, Hoffman and Feltovich (2004) Ten challenges for making automation a team player in joint human-agent activity (IEEE Intelligent Systems)
finding: Argues automation must be a good team player. Basic compact: parties agree to work together and keep each other informed. Needs interpredictability, common ground and directability. Lists ten challenges.
numbers: Not opened (publisher server returned an error). No data; position paper.
limits: Content stated from memory and the secondary page that cites it; the exact 'ten challenges' wording is unverified. Crossref confirmed title and DOI only.
agent_relevance: Three needs map to scaffold features: predictable steps, shared state visible to the user, and the user able to redirect. Test against Co-Gym failure modes.

source: Sarter, Woods and Billings (1997) Automation surprises (Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics, 2nd ed.)
finding: Automation surprise: the automation does something the operator did not expect, often from mode error and weak feedback. Only the Wikipedia stub definition was read.
numbers: The opened stub has no numbers and does not cite Sarter et al.
limits: The 1997 chapter was not opened. Do not cite its findings from this line.
agent_relevance: Hidden mode changes in a scaffold (a state the user cannot see) are the analogue. Keep state visible in the trace.

source: Hollnagel (2012) Coping with complexity: past, present and future (Cognition, Technology and Work)
finding: Retrospective by Hollnagel on how CSE grew from the need to cope with complexity in systems whose behaviour cannot be fully specified in advance.
numbers: Not opened (publisher redirected to a login).
limits: Only title and venue seen via secondary citation. No content claims to rely on.
agent_relevance: Pointer for follow-up in a later pass.
